summary: Describes a base solution and an experimental protocol to support mobile multicast senders in Proxy Mobile IPv6 domains. It defines optimizations such as synchronizing PMIPv6 with PIM and a peering function for MLD proxies, while the mobile sources remain unaware.

eli5.summary: A moving device wants to send a message to a whole group as it travels. This lets the network handle the hard parts so the device never has to notice.

questions: multicast sender in proxy mobile ipv6
subtitle: Enable mobile devices to send multicast while moving, transparently from the sender's perspective.

tldr.problem: Standard PMIPv6 networks support mobile receivers of multicast but not mobile senders. When a mobile node sends multicast, the network cannot route it properly through handovers, causing service disruption.
tldr.mechanism: This document extends PMIPv6 to support multicast senders through three complementary approaches: base solution with MLD proxy at access gateways, direct multicast routing at the access network, and MLD proxy peering for optimized source mobility.
tldr.outcome: Mobile nodes can send multicast data while moving without awareness of mobility operations. Support for both IPv4 and IPv6, with protocol optimizations for PIM-SM and BIDIR-PIM routing.

today: RFC 7287 is an Experimental specification published in June 2014. It provides comprehensive support for multicast senders in PMIPv6 domains across multiple deployment scenarios.

sections.title: Mobile Multicast Senders in PMIPv6
sections.content:
Proxy Mobile IPv6 (PMIPv6) enables mobile nodes to move between access networks without managing their own IP routing. The base PMIPv6 specification supports mobile receivers of multicast (through RFC 6224, which deploys MLD proxy functions), but it does not naturally support mobile senders.

When a mobile node sends multicast data, two problems arise. First, the network's routers may not know where the mobile sender is located, causing packets to be dropped before being delivered. Second, when the sender moves to a new access gateway during an ongoing multicast transmission, the multicast distribution trees used by routers become invalid, and packets are lost during the recovery period.

This document describes solutions to enable mobile multicast senders across three deployment scenarios: the base solution using MLD proxies (RFC 6224), direct multicast routing within the access network, and an optimized peering function for MLD proxies that improves routing efficiency.
sections.eli5: PMIPv6 works for people watching a broadcast. This lets people also be the ones sending the broadcast as they move.

sections.title: Base Solution: MLD Proxy at Access Gateways
sections.content:
In the base solution, Mobile Access Gateways (MAGs) are equipped with MLD proxy functions, similar to RFC 6224 but extended to handle sender mobility. A mobile node sends multicast packets to its current MAG as if it were on a fixed network. The MAG's MLD proxy forwards the packets upstream toward the Local Mobility Anchor (LMA), which acts as the multicast router and distributes the traffic to other mobile nodes and to the fixed Internet.

The critical feature is that when a mobile sender moves to a new MAG (handover), the sender continues sending with the same source address (its Home Network Prefix), but now through the new MAG. The new MAG's MLD proxy forwards the traffic upstream to the LMA using the tunnel to that LMA. Since the source address does not change, other routers in the network see only one source address and can establish normal multicast routes to the LMA.

However, the base solution has efficiency limitations. When two mobile nodes attached to the same MAG but served by different LMAs exchange multicast, traffic must travel up to one LMA, across to the other LMA, and back down to the same MAG—creating redundant paths. Additionally, receivers off the MAG must receive all traffic through the LMA, even when a more direct path exists.
sections.eli5: When a sender moves, packets go up to the LMA through the new gate. Receivers still get the traffic, but maybe not the fastest way.

sections.title: Direct Multicast Routing: PIM and BIDIR-PIM
sections.content:
To improve routing efficiency, multicast routing protocols such as PIM-SM (Protocol Independent Multicast - Sparse Mode) and BIDIR-PIM (Bidirectional PIM) can be deployed at the access gateways and Local Mobility Anchors. This allows the access network to route multicast independently of PMIPv6 unicast routing.

PIM-SM operates in phases. In phase one, a mobile source sends register messages to a Rendezvous Point (RP), which then distributes traffic down an RP-based tree. On handover, the new MAG begins registering with the RP again, resuming traffic distribution. In phases two and three, the RP attempts to build more direct shortest-path trees toward the source, but these require careful management during handovers because the source's attachment point has changed.

The specification provides handover optimizations for PIM-SM: when a source moves, the LMA can synchronize multicast state changes with unicast tunnel reconfiguration, ensuring that PIM (S,G) join states follow the source to its new MAG immediately.

BIDIR-PIM is simpler and more robust for mobile senders. It establishes spanning trees toward pre-configured Rendezvous Point Addresses. When a source moves, the new MAG (now the Designated Forwarder for the source) immediately forwards traffic onto the existing spanning tree without any protocol signaling or state recovery. BIDIR-PIM does not require tree rebuild on handover, making it the protocol of choice for access networks with mobile senders.
sections.eli5: PIM lets routers find good paths but needs to rebuild them when the sender moves. BIDIR-PIM has paths already built, so moving is instant.

sections.title: MLD Proxy Peering for Optimized Mobility
sections.content:
While MLD proxies at MAGs (base solution) are simple to deploy, they create inefficient paths when the source and receiver use different LMAs. To solve this without deploying full multicast routing, MLD proxy peering allows proxies at different MAGs to directly exchange multicast traffic.

Peering interfaces are configured as virtual links (either direct links or tunnels) between proxy instances at different MAGs. When a multicast packet arrives at a peering proxy from a locally attached source, the proxy checks whether another peering proxy has subscribers for that group. If so, the packet is sent directly to the peer proxy, avoiding the detour through the LMA.

Simple local filtering rules prevent routing loops and ensure each receiver receives the multicast stream only once. These rules are decidable at each proxy without requiring full multicast routing state or knowledge of the overall topology.

The peering function works with the base solution and can be deployed without changes to existing multicast protocols (IGMP/MLD or PIM). Mobile sources remain completely unaware that their traffic is being optimized.
sections.eli5: Two gates on the same network can swap broadcasts directly instead of sending them up and down through the center.

sections.title: IPv4 Support and Security
sections.content:
All three solutions (base, direct routing, and peering) support both IPv6 and IPv4 multicast. For IPv4, the network uses IGMP proxy functions at the MAG instead of MLD proxy, with identical operational procedures. Mobile nodes using IPv4 addresses transparently participate in multicast source mobility without any special behavior.

The specification notes that in dual-stack networks, different IPv4 and IPv6 multicast streams may be distributed for the same content, potentially causing duplicate delivery. Operators should coordinate address space usage and service bindings when deploying direct multicast routing scenarios.

Security and implementation aspects remain consistent across all solutions: multicast traffic inherits the security properties of the underlying transport (MLD, IGMP, PIM), and there is no requirement for mobility-specific security beyond what PMIPv6 already provides.
sections.eli5: IPv4 works the same way. The phone doesn't know anything is different from normal multicast.
